name: Belarusian
variety: Standard Belarusian (literary norm based on the central dialects around Minsk)
sources: Bird, Sonya & Litvin, Natallia (2021). Belarusian. Journal of the International Phonetic Association 51(3).
Mayo, Peter (1993). Belorussian. In B. Comrie & G. G. Corbett (eds.), The Slavonic Languages. London: Routledge.
Padlužny, A. I. (1989). Fanetyka belaruskaj litaraturnaj movy. Minsk: Navuka i tèchnika.
Czekman, Walery & Smułkowa, Elżbieta (1988). Fonetyka i fonologia języka białoruskiego z elementami fonetyki i fonologii ogólnej. Warszawa: PWN.
Vyhonnaja, L. C. (1991). Intanacyja. Nacisk. Arfaepija. Minsk: Navuka i tèchnika.
contrasts: palatalised versus non-palatalised consonants for labials, dentals, velars, /n/ and /l/
the soft partners of /t d/ are the affricates /t͡sʲ d͡zʲ/ (tsekanne and dzekanne: дзень, цень)
/r/, /t͡ʂ d͡ʐ/ and /ʂ ʐ/ are always hard (рака, рэчка, чысты)
fricative /ɣ/ is the regular reflex of г; the stop /ɡ/ occurs in few words (ганак, гузік)
long (geminate) consonants between vowels, mostly soft (калоссе [kaˈɫɔsʲːɛ], жыццё [ʐɨˈt͡sʲːɔ], ноччу)
position of stress is lexically contrastive
allophony: akanne: /ɔ/ and /ɛ/ occur only under stress; in unstressed syllables they are replaced by [a], and the spelling shows this (малако, рака)
jakanne: after soft consonants /ɛ/ and /ɔ/ of the first pretonic syllable are replaced by [a], written я (зямля, вясна)
unstressed [a] is shorter and somewhat centralised but stays an open vowel in all unstressed positions (no second degree of reduction to [ə] as in Russian)
/v/ and historical /l/ are the glide [w] (written ў) after a vowel before a consonant or word-finally (воўк, праўда, быў)
word-final obstruents are devoiced (хлеб [xlʲɛp], снег [sʲnʲɛx]); obstruent clusters take the voicing of their last member (казка [ˈkaska], просьба [ˈprɔzʲba])
regressive assimilation of palatalisation: dental fricatives are soft before soft consonants (снег [sʲnʲɛx], дзве [d͡zʲvʲɛ])
sibilant assimilation: с, з before ш, ж, ч become [ʂ ʐ]
/ɫ/ is dental and velarised; /r/ is an alveolar trill
phonotactics: only [a], [i]/[ɨ] and [u] occur regularly in unstressed syllables of native words
no voiced obstruents before a pause
geminates from consonant plus /j/ between vowels
word-initial clusters starting with a sonorant may take a prothetic vowel (аржаны, імгла)

stress.rule: Stress can fall on any syllable and may shift within a paradigm; ordinary spelling does not mark it, but о and э (after hard consonants) and ё are normally found only in stressed syllables.
stress.cues: duration, intensity and vowel quality (the mid vowels occur only under stress)

rhythm.vowel_reduction: moderate: mid vowels are neutralised to [a] in unstressed syllables (akanne, jakanne), but unstressed vowels keep a fuller quality than in Russian
rhythm.notes: The rhythm class is an impression from the descriptive literature; no rhythm-metric study is cited.

length.notes: No phonemic vowel length. Long consonants occur between vowels (насенне, калоссе, збожжа) and are written double.

intonation.declarative: rising or high accents on non-final stressed syllables, fall to low on the nuclear stressed syllable
intonation.yes_no_question: rise on the stressed syllable of the word in focus followed by a fall; the particle ці may introduce the question
intonation.wh_question: high accent on the question word, then falling
intonation.continuation: rise on the last stressed syllable of the non-final phrase
intonation.accent_shape: rising accents before the nucleus; falling nuclear accent in statements
intonation.notes: Described on the basis of the reference works; close to the East Slavic pattern described for Russian.

tone.notes: No lexical tone or pitch accent.

problems: Stress: there is no stress dictionary. The letters о and ё are given primary stress by rule (correct for Belarusian spelling); every word without them is stressed on the first syllable, which is often wrong (вада, галава, зямля, вясна, сястра, рака all have final stress).

Soft consonants other than sʲ, zʲ, t͡sʲ, d͡zʲ are coded as the hard consonant plus a phoneme [;] that has no sound data in the Belarusian table: there is no palatal transition into the following vowel (in нёс the vowel starts with the same formants as in нос) and almost no difference word-finally (конь, соль, быль).
No fronted vowel allophones after soft consonants.
Voicing assimilation and final devoicing are letter rules that look only inside the word; nothing is assimilated between a preposition and the next word.
Long consonants are coded only for цц, чч, шш; other geminates are two separate consonants (калоссе [sʲsʲ]).
Only the default eSpeak tunes are used; wh-questions get the same fall-rise as yes-no questions.
good: г is the fricative [ɣ], devoiced to [x] word-finally
ў is [w]; р, ч, ш, ж are hard (retroflex phonemes)
dzekanne and tsekanne affricates /d͡zʲ t͡sʲ/ have their own phonemes
final devoicing and voicing assimilation inside words (хлеб, дуб, казка, просьба)
assimilative softening of с, з before soft consonants (снег [sʲnʲɛx])
no extra vowel reduction is applied, which suits the akanne-based spelling

notes: No formant, VOT or rhythm-metric values are given because I cannot quote published figures with confidence.
